lines.text: Run the exact same query, over the exact same table, on two different engines, and they agree on the answer down to a rounding error.
One of them takes well over three seconds.
The other finishes in about a quarter of a second.
Same table, same SQL, same answer, checked and not assumed.
Why would one engine take sixteen times longer than the other to produce it?
Not the hardware, and not a smarter plan — both engines pick the same kind of scan, filter and group.
What differs is how many rows actually move through each step of getting there at once.
The slower engine's executor works by asking the operator below it for one row, getting exactly one row back, and asking again.
Every operator in the plan, for every single row, pulled one at a time, all the way from the bottom to the top.
Pulling one row at a time means calling a function, once, for every operator, for every one of those millions of rows.
That's not free. Each call is its own small overhead, and it also hides any chance for the processor to work on more than one row at once.
Millions of tiny function calls add up to a real, measurable cost.
The faster engine's operators don't take one row at a time.
They take a whole array of rows in a single call.
A couple thousand rows move through one operator call, instead of one.
Instead of calling a function once per row, a vectorized operator runs one tight loop over an array already sitting in the processor's cache.
Same filter, same arithmetic, same millions of rows underneath.
Just looped over in batches, instead of summoned one at a time.
A batch of a couple thousand rows clearly beats a batch of one.
Does an even bigger batch keep winning — would the whole table in one call beat that?
No — there's a sweet spot.
A batch only helps as long as it still fits inside the cache it's actually processed in. Past that, bigger stops helping and starts hurting.
On the benchmark that first measured this: a batch of exactly one row ran about as slowly as a plain row-at-a-time interpreter.
The best size measured was in the low thousands, with a wide range on either side still working fine.
Go past that range, though, and the batch no longer fits the cache, and the time climbs right back up again.
There's a way to go further than batching rows into arrays.
Compile the whole plan — the scan, the filter, the hash build — into one piece of actual machine code.
Values stay inside the processor's own registers the whole way through, pushed forward instead of pulled, instead of ever being written out to an array in between.

tolerated.line: There's a way to go further than batching rows into arrays.

lines.text: Three ways to run the exact same plan, on one core: pull one row at a time, process a batch at a time, or compile the whole thing to machine code first.
Which one actually wins?
Compiling — it removes the most overhead of the three, by cutting out both the per-row call and the per-batch bookkeeping.
But winning on raw speed isn't the same as winning for free.
The system that pioneered this found hand-written code and its own compiled output landing close together — both a long way ahead of a plain row-at-a-time interpreter.
That speed comes with a real cost on the other side, though.

Every query first has to be compiled into machine code before its very first row comes out, and once something goes wrong inside that generated code, it's a much harder thing to read than a plain interpreter loop.

tolerated.line: The system that pioneered this found hand-written code and its own compiled output landing close together — both a long way ahead of a plain row-at-a-time interpreter.

lines.text: There's one more piece: how work gets spread across more than one core.
Instead of deciding the number of threads before a query even starts, split the work into small pieces and hand each idle thread the next piece as it finishes the last one.
Measured directly here: going from one thread to four cut the time by well over a factor of three — the same kind of scaling the system that introduced this idea reported at a much larger scale.
Pulling one row at a time costs a function call for every single row.
A batch amortizes that call, as long as it still fits in cache.
Compiling removes even the batch, at the price of compiling before you start and of a much harder debugging story.
And a fixed number of threads is just another decision made too early — morsels make it at run time instead.

lines.text: A plan reports one row count for an entire stage of work, not one line for every row that passed through it.
Does that sound like an engine pulling rows one at a time, or one working in batches?
Working in batches.
An engine that's only ever handling one row at a time has no reason to report a count for a whole stage at once — that kind of reporting is a sign it's accounting for arrays, not individual rows.
One engine's time drops by well over a factor of three, going from one thread to four, on the very same work.
Does that look like elastic, run-time scheduling, or a split that was fixed before the query even started?
Elastic, run-time scheduling.
Scaling that closely tracks the number of cores actually available is exactly what a fixed, decided-in-advance split wouldn't give you on a different machine.
